why: Keeping the k largest values seen so far in a size-k min-heap means the heap top is always the kth largest: a direct top-k heap problem (quickselect is the alternative).
hints: You do not need the whole array sorted, only the boundary between the top k and the rest.
Keep a min-heap of the k largest elements so far. When it grows beyond k, pop the smallest. At the end the heap top is the kth largest.
heapq push/pop per element: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Quickselect gives average O(n).
pitfalls: Duplicates count separately: in [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6] with k = 4 the answer is 4, not 3.
Python's heapq is a min-heap; for a max-heap approach you must negate values.
